detailed_summary: The paper addresses the gap between quantum decoding success (matching the logical class of an error) and ordered-statistics decoding (OSD), which searches a finite list of physical corrections. It introduces a rank-k logical-signature map M_log: F_2^q -> F_2^k that projects physical error patterns onto their logical class. For fixed, error-independent orderings, the authors derive the exact logical-signature distribution, the OSD-0 logical error rate, and the logical-class coverage of any fixed list. For minimum-cost list decoding, they prove a decomposition P_L = P_miss + P_sel, separating failures due to absent logical classes from wrong representative selection. The framework is validated on hypergraph-product and bivariate-bicycle codes, and on the [[144,12,12]] gross code. Notably, 672 coverage-aware candidates outperform 899 combination-sweep candidates (McNemar p=0.013), and two lists with identical logical coverage yield logical error rates of 11.30% and 3.78%, demonstrating that coverage alone is insufficient. The signature-based coverage compression persists across 30 random column orderings. The work concludes that logical coverage and within-class representative selection are complementary resources, and provides a framework to guide OSD list construction and compression.
key_contributions: Introduces a rank-k logical-signature map M_log that connects physical error patterns to logical classes, enabling exact computation of logical-signature distributions and OSD-0 logical error rates for fixed orderings.
Proves a decomposition P_L = P_miss + P_sel for minimum-cost list decoding, separating failures due to missing logical classes from wrong representative selection.
Derives the logical-class coverage of any fixed list and shows how coverage-aware candidate selection can outperform larger lists chosen by combination sweeps.

Demonstrates on the [[144,12,12]] gross code that 672 coverage-aware candidates achieve lower logical error rate than 899 combination-sweep candidates (p=0.013), and that identical coverage can yield vastly different P_L (11.30% vs 3.78%).

Shows that signature-based coverage compression is robust across 30 random column orderings, and provides a framework for OSD list construction and compression by identifying coverage requirements and distinguishing coverage losses from representative selection failures.
methodology_analysis: The authors develop a theoretical framework based on linear algebra over F_2. They define a logical-signature map M_log that maps a physical error vector to its logical class (a k-bit syndrome-like signature). For a fixed ordering of columns (qubits), they compute the exact distribution of logical signatures by enumerating all error patterns up to a given weight or by dynamic programming. This yields the OSD-0 logical error rate (when only the most likely error is considered) and the coverage of any list of candidate corrections. For minimum-cost list decoding, they prove that the logical error probability decomposes into P_miss (the probability that the true logical class is not represented in the list) and P_sel (the probability that the decoder selects a wrong representative from the correct class). The methodology is validated on two code families: hypergraph-product codes and bivariate-bicycle codes, including the [[144,12,12]] gross code. They compare coverage-aware candidate selection (using the signature map to ensure coverage of likely logical classes) against combination-sweep selection (a heuristic that generates candidates by flipping combinations of low-reliability bits). They perform paired McNemar tests to assess statistical significance and test robustness across 30 random column orderings.
results_analysis: The key results are: (1) For fixed orderings, the exact logical-signature distribution and OSD-0 logical error rate can be computed, and the coverage of any list can be determined. (2) The decomposition P_L = P_miss + P_sel is proven and validated. (3) On the [[144,12,12]] gross code, a coverage-aware list of 672 candidates achieves a lower logical error rate than a combination-sweep list of 899 candidates, with a paired McNemar p-value of 0.013, indicating statistical significance. (4) Two lists with identical logical coverage (i.e., same set of logical classes represented) yield drastically different logical error rates: 11.30% and 3.78%, showing that within-class representative selection is crucial. (5) The coverage compression effect persists across 30 random column orderings, suggesting robustness. These results highlight that candidate count alone is not a good predictor of performance; both coverage and selection quality matter.
strengths: Provides a rigorous theoretical framework that bridges physical error patterns and logical classes, enabling exact analysis of OSD and list decoding.
The decomposition P_L = P_miss + P_sel offers a clear diagnostic tool to distinguish between coverage failures and selection failures.
Empirical validation on a realistic quantum code ([[144,12,12]] gross code) with statistical testing (McNemar) and robustness checks across random orderings.
Demonstrates a counterintuitive result: fewer candidates can outperform more candidates when chosen with coverage awareness, challenging conventional wisdom.
limitations: The framework assumes fixed, error-independent orderings; it does not address adaptive or error-dependent orderings, which are common in practice.
The analysis is limited to minimum-cost list decoding and OSD-0; extensions to higher-order OSD or more complex decoders are not explored.
The empirical validation is primarily on one code family (bivariate-bicycle) and one specific code; broader testing across diverse quantum LDPC codes would strengthen generality.
connections_to_research: This work is directly relevant to quantum error correction and fault-tolerant quantum computing, core topics in quantum physics. It provides a deeper understanding of decoding failures in quantum LDPC codes, which are leading candidates for practical quantum memories. The logical-signature map and the P_L decomposition offer new tools for analyzing and improving decoders, potentially impacting the design of efficient decoders for near-term quantum devices. The focus on OSD, a widely used decoder for quantum LDPC codes, makes the results immediately applicable to ongoing efforts in quantum error correction.
overall_assessment: The paper presents a novel and rigorous framework that connects physical error patterns to logical classes, yielding both theoretical insights and practical decoder improvements. The proof of the P_L decomposition and the demonstration that coverage-aware selection can outperform larger lists are significant contributions. The empirical results on the [[144,12,12]] gross code are compelling, though limited to one code family. The work is of high quality and likely to influence future decoder design and analysis in quantum error correction.
